clue.text: Other halves dropping by, look to have made port

indicators.note: other halves dropping says one half of each word goes: the front halves of the first three words, the back halves of the last two

parts.note: the five words taken as written

explanation.surface: Partners pop in and look to have arrived at a harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Other halves' suggests spouses, but it is halves of words: by, look, to keep Y, OK, O, and have, made keep HA, MA, their other halves dropping.
explanation.definitionFit: Yokohama is a major Japanese seaport on Tokyo Bay.

clue.text: Pro on strike picked up regular

parts.note: pro means in favour of

indicators.note: in a Down clue, picked up means lifted, so the word reads from the bottom upwards

parts.note: lam means to beat or hit

explanation.surface: A professional on picket duty is taken back on as a regular worker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' places the first piece above the second in a Down answer. Thematically, GO goes before 'on strike'.
explanation.definitionFit: Formal and regular both mean following established rules or conventional form, as in a formal or regular arrangement.

clue.text: Old sacred book in residence gets conned by man without cap

parts.note: up means in residence at a university

indicators.note: removing a cap takes off the top, which in a word is its first letter

parts.note: taken as written
is had, is taken in or fooled

explanation.surface: A student in halls is cheated by a bareheaded man out of an ancient holy text.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' in British usage means attending university, especially Oxford or Cambridge. 'by' puts the shortened man next to the swindle.
explanation.definitionFit: The Upanishads are ancient Sanskrit philosophical scriptures of Hinduism, so each is an old sacred text.

clue.text: Dominican horse accommodated by fine German home

indicators.note: something accommodated is housed, so it goes within the other letters

parts.note: ja is German for yes, all right
in means at home
a cob is a sturdy short-legged horse

explanation.surface: A horse from the Dominican Republic is stabled at a decent German house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dominican' looks Caribbean; it is the friar. French Dominicans were called Jacobins after their Paris church of St Jacques.
explanation.definitionFit: Jacobin was the French name for a Dominican friar, from their convent of Saint-Jacques in Paris.

clue.text: Bust Assam plant

indicators.note: something bust is broken, so the next word's letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A tea estate in Assam has gone bankrupt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plant' suggests a tea factory or bush; it is a tree.
explanation.definitionFit: The msasa is a southern African tree of the miombo woodlands, so it is a plant.

clue.text: Rambling around at East Peak with West Park behind

indicators.note: around means turned about, so the little word before the compass point is read backwards
rambling means wandering aimlessly, so the letters of the mountain word are rearranged

parts.note: E is the compass abbreviation for east
W is the compass abbreviation for west

explanation.surface: A walker wanders about at East Peak, with West Park lying behind.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites scrambling all of 'at East Peak', but the compass points stay put: 'around' acts only on the little word before them, and 'Rambling' only on the mountain. 'Park behind' is slang for settling your bottom on a seat.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a casual idiom for sitting down, literally finding a church bench to rest your rear on.

clue.text: Himalayan native was transmitting about leaving India

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the phrase is read in the opposite direction
leaving means departing, so a letter goes out

parts.note: radioed, sent a message by radio
India is I in the phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A local from the Himalayas was broadcasting about leaving India.
explanation.walkthrough: 'native' suggests a person; it is a tree native to the region.
explanation.definitionFit: The deodar is a cedar that grows wild in the western Himalayas, so it is a native there.

clue.text: Impossible to describe other Across answers (or words in Down clues)?

parts.words: to describe other Across answers (or words in Down clues)?
parts.note: surface reading: a phrase too hard to pin down the rest of the grid; setter's reading: every other Across answer, and a word in each Down clue, makes a phrase once the second word of this answer goes in front of it

explanation.surface: A solver despairs that the rest of the puzzle defies description.
explanation.walkthrough: This is the theme key: put GO before each Across answer (go pear-shaped, go commando, go steady, go ballistic, go bananas, go Dutch, go hang) or before a word in each Down clue (go halves, go on strike).
explanation.definitionFit: A no-go area or plan is one that cannot be entered or carried out, so the phrase means not possible.

clue.text: Soft-spoken journo pursuing crackpot perhaps with a cutting

indicators.note: cutting means slicing into, so the single letter goes inside the word before it
a crackpot is a crazy person, so the following words are scrambled into a mad arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
the article taken as written
ED, short for editor, a journalist

explanation.surface: A quiet reporter trails some crank who might be carrying a newspaper cutting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pursuing' puts the journalist after the scrambled letters. 'Soft' looks like P for piano, but it belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A pear-shaped voice, in old-fashioned use, is rich, rounded and mellow in tone, as of someone softly and carefully spoken.

clue.text: Soldier Bill's partner punched by chap visiting medic

indicators.note: a word punched by another has that other driven into its middle

parts.note: in the phrase 'bill and coo', coo goes with bill

indicators.note: someone visiting is staying inside another's place, so one word goes within the other

parts.note: MD, Doctor of Medicine
a chap is a man

explanation.surface: A soldier is thumped by a man calling at the doctor's, while Bill's other half looks on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a person; it is a bird's beak, and lovers 'bill and coo'. The chap sits inside the medic, and that pair goes inside COO.
explanation.definitionFit: A commando is a soldier in a unit trained for raids, so the word names a kind of soldier.

clue.text: Guy (or lady) finally selected after assorted dates?

indicators.note: assorted things are mixed up, so the word that follows has its letters jumbled

parts.note: the letters of dates rearranged

indicators.note: finally points to the very end of the word just before it in the clue

parts.note: the final letter of lady

explanation.surface: Someone chooses a partner after a series of trial dates.
explanation.walkthrough: '(or lady)' does double duty: it widens the definition to either sex and also supplies the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A steady is a regular boyfriend or girlfriend, someone you are going out with exclusively.

clue.text: Projected flight's line initially includes southern parts of Latvia?

indicators.note: to part something is to split it, so these letters are pushed in between

parts.note: Latvia is a Baltic state, so belonging to Latvia is Baltic

indicators.note: only the opening letter of includes is taken

explanation.surface: Asks whether a flight path in Latvia first takes in its southern regions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'parts' is a verb, not a noun, splitting the adjective for Latvia.
explanation.definitionFit: Ballistics is the science of projectiles in flight, so the adjective describes a thrown or fired object's trajectory.

clue.text: Lean over

definitions.meaning: first meaning: thin, with no excess flesh
second meaning: left over, surplus to needs

explanation.walkthrough: The two words read like an instruction to bend across something; they are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective covers a gaunt, thin figure and also anything extra or remaining, like a spare tyre.

clue.text: Foolishly compare KFC with a losing company, loads attached to it?

indicators.note: foolishly means the letters are arranged in a silly new order
losing means the letters for company are taken out of the jumbled pool

explanation.surface: A daft comparison between a fast-food chain and a failing firm weighed down by its debts.
explanation.walkthrough: Take COMPARE KFC A, 'losing' CO for company, and arrange the rest 'foolishly'. The definition is cryptic: it describes the answer as a thing that loads are fixed to.
explanation.definitionFit: A packframe is a rigid frame worn on the back to which a pack or other loads are strapped for carrying.

clue.text: Crazy fool cracks down in Marseille

indicators.note: to crack something is to break into it, so one word ends up inside the other

parts.note: bas is French for low or down, and Marseille is in France
nana is British slang for a silly person

explanation.surface: A crazy fool smashes something up somewhere in the south of France.
explanation.walkthrough: A nana is British slang for a fool. 'in Marseille' tells you to translate 'down' into French.
explanation.definitionFit: Bananas is informal slang for mad, as in going bananas, so it is a synonym of crazy.

clue.text: Naturally resulting current bankrupt charges wound golf clubs

parts.note: AC, alternating current

indicators.note: to charge is to load or fill, so one piece fills the other
wound, as in wound back, means turned the other way

parts.note: golf is G in the phonetic alphabet
C for clubs, the card suit
to ruin someone is to bankrupt them

explanation.surface: A broke player's current fees are wiped out to cover damaged golf equipment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'golf clubs' reads as a set of sticks but is two letters, turned round, holding the bankruptcy.
explanation.definitionFit: Interest that is accruing is building up as a natural consequence, the dictionary sense of resulting naturally.

clue.text: Binder much further up, according to Spooner

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so W and H change places

parts.note: way is an intensifier meaning much, as in 'way better'
higher means further up, and it is said like 'hire'

explanation.surface: Someone describes a thing as much further up the slope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Way higher' with first sounds swapped gives the binding wire for bales.
explanation.definitionFit: Haywire is the wire used to tie bales of hay, so it binds them.

clue.text: Such dishevelment may put out hungry amigo

indicators.note: put out means disturbed, so the letters of hungry amigo are rearranged once the word may is taken from them

explanation.surface: A starving Spanish-speaking friend may be upset by such a ruffled appearance.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the clue backwards: the answer together with MAY, put out, would give HUNGRY AMIGO. So remove M, A and Y from HUNGRY AMIGO and rearrange the remaining letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Roughing up hair or feathers ruffles them, so this word names the act of making something untidy and dishevelled.

clue.text: Eccentric participants in chess, players who may be out on a limb?

definitions.text: players who may be out on a limb?

parts.note: bats is informal for crazy
chess pieces are called men

explanation.surface: Odd chess players who might end up isolated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out on a limb' means isolated, but in cricket a batter can be out leg before wicket, LBW, with the leg (a limb) in front of the stumps.
explanation.definitionFit: Batsmen are cricket players, and one may be dismissed LBW, out on account of a leg.

clue.text: Wife of King Willem-Alexander?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Cockney slang for a wife, short for duchess
second meaning: belonging to the monarch's country, the Netherlands

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a question about the Dutch queen. In Cockney slang 'my old Dutch' (from duchess) is a man's wife; Willem-Alexander is King of the Netherlands.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a Cockney term for one's wife and also the adjective for the Netherlands and its king.

clue.text: Agreement is not acceptable, having to round it up

indicators.note: having to go round something means enclosing it
in a Down clue, up means the word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: non-U, not upper-class, so socially unacceptable
taken as written

explanation.surface: A deal is rejected, and has to be wrapped up again.
explanation.walkthrough: Non-U is British slang, from the 1950s, for speech or behaviour not used by the upper class.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting in unison means acting together in agreement, so unison is concord or accord.

clue.text: Royal PR exercise OK, but a law gets broken

indicators.note: a broken law is shattered, so the words before are smashed and reassembled

parts.note: the letters of these four words

explanation.surface: A palace publicity stunt goes fine, though some regulation is breached in the process.
explanation.definitionFit: A walkabout is an informal stroll by royalty among crowds, staged to meet the public.

clue.text: Happy books at introduction Harriett dips into live

indicators.note: dips into means goes inside, so these letters sit within the word for live

parts.note: to be is to live or exist
lit, short for literature

indicators.note: an introduction is the start, so only the opening letter of the name is used

parts.note: the first letter of the name

explanation.surface: A cheerful Harriett dips into books at the opening of a live event.
explanation.definitionFit: Blithe means carefree and cheerful, a literary synonym of happy.

clue.text: Muscular chef's left cold turkey with no stuffing

indicators.note: left as in departed, so a letter has gone from the word

parts.note: the 's is 'has'
C for cold, as on a tap

indicators.note: without its stuffing only the outside of the word remains

parts.note: the first and last letters of turkey

explanation.surface: A brawny cook has abandoned a cold turkey that was not stuffed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cold turkey' reads as a phrase about quitting a habit; the two words are split, C and the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Hefty means big and strong, so it describes a muscular build.

clue.text: Think Formula One drive's good now leading

parts.note: F for formula and I, the Roman one

indicators.note: the letter for good now goes to the front, rearranging the word it sits in

parts.note: a drive is an urge; the 's is 'has'

explanation.surface: A motorsport driver reckons the car is going well and is in the lead now.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Formula One' looks like motor racing but is two letters. In URGE the G (good) moves to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: To figure is to suppose or reckon, as in 'I figure he's right', so it means to think.

clue.text: Great many taking pictures back in hand

indicators.note: taking means holding something within, so one word is put inside another

parts.note: a sight of something is a great deal of it, as in 'a sight better'

indicators.note: back means the word for pictures is read from its end

parts.note: pictures are art

explanation.surface: A lot of photographs are held back in someone's hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hand' is a card hand, not a body part.
explanation.definitionFit: In poker a straight is a hand of five cards in sequence, so it is a kind of hand.

clue.text: With current trends having fluctuated before noon, it pained me to butt in

indicators.note: to butt in is to interrupt, so the cry of pain pushes into the other letters
having fluctuated means the letters of trends have shifted about into a new order

parts.note: AM, ante meridiem, means before noon
ow is the cry of someone who has been hurt

explanation.surface: A trader complains that watching market trends swing about all morning was painful to sit through.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having fluctuated' turns TRENDS into DNSTRE; AM follows, and OW, the exclamation of pain, 'butts in' after the D. Current looks like a word about the present day, but it is a flow of water.
explanation.definitionFit: Downstream means in the same direction as a river's flow, so travelling along with the current.

clue.text: This exhibit in church would represent transition

indicators.note: this points at the answer itself, the thing that would be placed inside the church letters
the clue says the answer placed in the church letters makes the word for transition, so those church letters come out of it

parts.note: a change is a transition from one state to another
CE, Church of England, is a standard abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: A curator muses that putting this exhibit inside a church would mark a change of direction.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue runs backwards: the answer placed 'in' CE would make CHANGE, so take CE out of CHANGE.
explanation.definitionFit: To hang a painting is to put it on display, so the verb means to show or exhibit art.
